catalog_quote: In normal speech the main word stress falls on the penultimate syllable, as in Malay, with minor stress on the final syllable (Lewis 1947:18). When the penultimate syllable is a pre-syllable, this is unstressed, and the major stress falls on the last syllable. Pre-syllables do not normally have any stress and the amount of transition (i.e. its vocalic clarity, length and prominence) is conditioned by the speed and rhythm of the phrase and ranges from zero to an unstressed [ə]. ... The rule that pre-syllables do not carry stress has three exceptions, the words /demiq/ 'small', /deniya/ 'world' and /semengac/ 'spirit'. ... In tri-syllabic words there is a potential minor stress on the first syllable, when that syllable is the prefix /ber-/ /per-/ or /ter/. ... new_statements.quote: Stress in Urak Lawoi' is predictable. [...] In monosyllabic words, stress is actually on the peak of that syllable. [...] In disyllabic words of which a presyllable is the first syllable, stress is on the last syllable. [...] In disyllabic words of which a minor syllable is the first syllable, stress is on both syllables: primary stress on the last syllable and secondary stress on the first syllable. [...] it should be concluded that the words in Urak Lawoi' bear only one heavy stress, i.e. on the peak of monosyllabic words and on the last syllable of disyllabic and trisyllabic words. In actual high speed utterances, the secondary stress may be dropped, leaving only one primary stress as concluded above.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Urak Lawoi' has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this source supplies the rule (fixed final primary stress, secondary stress on preceding minor syllables, presyllable/minor/major syllable distinction). scanned text: 'syllabie' etc. are scanned errors for 'syllable'; the quote is normalised only at those characters.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable and non-contrastive: primary stress always falls on the last syllable of the phonological word (one to three syllables). Words are built of an obligatory final major syllable preceded by optional presyllables (no contrastive vowel, unstressed) and minor syllables (full vowel, secondary stress). Author recommends omitting stress from phonemic writing.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every minor syllable preceding the final major syllable: on the first syllable of minor+major disyllables (e.g. [ˌka'cak] 'bean'), on the second syllable of presyllable+minor+major trisyllables (e.g. [se ˌpu'luh] 'ten'), on both non-final syllables of minor+minor+major trisyllables; presyllables carry no stress; secondary stress may drop in fast speech.
new_statements.exceptions: None; stress is stated to be fully predictable. Pitch (three levels, high/mid/low) is described separately as a property of the stress group (section 2.2.3 ff.), not as contrastive tone on words.
new_statements.identity_note: Saengmani 1979 describes the Adang Island variety (Satun province); Hogan 1976 describes Urak Lawoi' of Phuket and the Adang islands and notes only slight dialect variation between them. Steinhauer 2008 (not opened) treats Urak Lawoi' as a distinct Malayic variety; its abstract is about diachronic sound changes, not stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No explicit stress rule is stated, but the word is defined as an obligatory main (major) syllable that is always last, preceded by up to two minor syllables (which can carry a stress) and/or pre-syllables (no contrastive vowel, at most a weak stress in phrase-final position). This is the same final-major-syllable structure that Saengmani 1979 spells out as final primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Minor syllables have 'the potential for a stress'; pre-syllable transitions range from zero to weak stress. No primary/secondary terminology.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Notes slight variation between the Urak Lawoi' of Phuket and of the Adang islands (p. 284), not concerning stress.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Urak Lawoi' has an empty rule and there are no existing_statements, so nothing is contradicted; the work adds only a second-hand, conditional remark (heavy /ər/ penult bears 'the major word stress', per Hogan and Pattemore 1988: 18) plus an acknowledgement of secondary stress. It does not supply a placement rule. 2.2 pp. 18-20) states primary stress on the last syllable with secondary stress on preceding minor syllables and none on presyllables; Hogan 1976 (PL C-43: 284, Phuket older-generation dialect) says that when minor and main syllables co-occur 'the stress falls evenly on both in citation form' and the pre-syllable has no stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The article is a historical phonology of Urak Lawoi' (sound changes from Proto-Malayic, based on Hogan's dictionary and Hogan and Pattemore 1988); it has no stress/prosody section and states no general rule of word-stress placement. The only stress remark is incidental: Steinhauer quotes Hogan and Pattemore (1988: 18) that a penultimate syllable containing lengthened schwa (Hogan's /ər/) 'bears the major word stress', and he himself attributes the optional extra r in spellings like krerja/trerbeq to 'vowel lengthening in stressed or secondary stressed position'. This presupposes that Urak Lawoi' has word stress (major and secondary) and that a heavy /ər/ penult can carry the major stress, but gives no default placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentions 'secondary stressed position' in passing (p. 121) without saying where secondary stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as such; the penult-stress remark is restricted to penults with lengthened schwa (/ər/).
new_statements.identity_note: Steinhauer 2008 works from Hogan's materials, which describe the older-generation Phuket Island dialect (Hogan 1976 notes slight Phuket/Phi Phi vs. other-islands and generational variation); Saengmani 1979 describes the Adang Island dialect.

readall_conflicts: Steinhauer 2008 itself states no placement rule; its one stress remark (p. 121), quoted from Hogan and Pattemore 1988: 18, says a penultimate syllable with lengthened schwa (/ər/) 'bears the major word stress'. That sits in mild tension with the dedicated stress description held by the project, Saengmani 1979 (sec. 2.2, pp. 18-20: 'primary stress on the last syllable', secondary stress on preceding minor syllables, presyllables unstressed, 'the words in Urak Lawoi' bear only one heavy stress, i.e. on.. the last syllable of disyllabic and trisyllabic words'), and with Hogan 1976 (PL C-43 p. 284: main syllable is always word-final; with a minor syllable present 'the stress falls evenly on both in citation form'; pre-syllables carry no stress). The three are reconcilable if minor (full-vowel or /ər/) non-final syllables carry a secondary or level stress while the final main syllable carries the primary one, with Hogan and Pattemore's 'major word stress' on /ər/ penults being either a weight-driven exception or a different judgement of relative prominence; Steinhauer does not settle.

audit.recode_to: Keep the robust core (schwa pre-syllables unstressable; stress confined to the last two syllables; pre-syllable penult => final stress) but mark default primary-stress position as contested penult~final: Hogan 1988 (POP dialect) penult-main/final-minor 'as in Malay (Lewis 1947)'; Hogan 1976 (POP) even stress on both; Amon 1979 (Adang dialect, dedicated phonology) final-primary/penult-secondary, under which the record would be fixed: final syllable rather than 'weight'. At minimum add Amon 1979 and Hogan 1976 to sources/contra with a caution line; if the catalog must pick one value, final-primary with unstressable pre-syllables is the analysis shared by the dedicated phonology and consistent with Hogan's own 'clause stress falls on the last syllable'.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the PL-C109 text we hold at sec. 2.3.3, pp. 26-27 (lines 1607-1655). sources.quote: 'Stress in Urak Lawoi' is predictable.' Disyllables with a pre-syllable first: 'stress is on the last syllable' [be'nan]. Disyllables with a minor syllable first: 'primary stress on the last syllable and secondary stress on the first syllable' [,ka'cak], [,ma'ta] 'eye'. Trisyllables pre+minor+major: primary on last, secondary on second [se,pu'luh]; two pre-syllables + major: 'only one stress on the last syllable'; minor+minor+major: secondary on first two, primary on last [,ta,ma'ta] 'policeman'. 'it should be concluded that the words in Urak Lawoi' bear only one heavy stress, i.e. on the peak
sources.note: Only dedicated phonology of the language that is openly available; its stress-group chapter puts primary stress on the FINAL syllable (secondary on preceding full-vowel syllables), against Hogan 1988's penult-main claim on which our classification rests.
